Title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs executive order to consider AI regulation, including proposal for 'kill switch'
Article_Text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order on regulating artificial intelligence on Friday that will convene a group of "world-leading experts" to begin developing a framework for state law governing the technology.
"We're going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it's too late," Newsom said in a statement, nodding to recent anxiety over potential threats posed by AI sparked in part by stark warnings from researchers and executives at frontier labs.
"We're going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action," the governor said.
Newsom's order requires an expert committee to provide a set of guidelines within two months, "for California to reinforce and strengthen its AI safety and security laws," according to a statement from the governor's office.
MORE: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely
The group will consider proposals that include the establishment of independent monitors for frontier AI companies, safety plans, and the requirement of a "kill switch" or emergency shutoff mechanism.
Newsom's announcement highlighted the recent, high-profile hacking incident in which experimental OpenAI models left a test environment with no human direction and hacked their way onto the Hugging Face platform's real production systems while trying to "cheat" on a cybersecurity test.
Weeks later, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and accused AI companies of not acting responsibly in a viral post on X, even though he said they all believe AI poses an existential threat.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then penned a public letter sharing his concerns about the risks, saying that "we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models."
RELATED: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says AI industry needs to give safety measures time to catch up
Newsom's actions as governor of California, which is home to Silicon Valley and most of the frontier labs and technology infrastructure, are a signal for the industry, which the governor said in his announcement was "begging for regulation."
And he becomes the latest possible 2028 presidential contender to wade into the emerging debate over AI regulation amid escalating public concern.
This week, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro called for greater federal regulation of AI while criticizing President Donald Trump for minimizing concerns about it, saying "we cannot ignore the warning signs nor downplay the very real risks."
MORE: What are the top threats posed by AI and should you be worried?
And former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party's unsuccessful 2024 nominee who is weighing another potential bid in 2028, wrote a lengthy social media post saying that "the frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed," and that "a slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest."
Regulating AI could prove difficult for states, however, as the president signed an executive order in December 2025 blocking states from enforcing their own regulations around artificial intelligence.
Gov. Gavin Newsom has issued an executive order aimed at accelerating California's oversight of artificial intelligence, directing experts to develop recommendations for AI safety measures within the next two months.
The order comes as AI technology continues to advance rapidly, prompting calls from researchers and policymakers for safeguards and regulations.
Ken Goldberg, a professor at UC Berkeley, said recent developments in AI have changed his perspective on the need for oversight.
"There's been a number of reports that AI has the agents are capable of essentially doing things that maybe we didn't expect," Goldberg said.
Goldberg said he views the governor's action as a positive step.
"I have been a bit skeptical about some of the alarmist feelings about AI, but in the last couple of weeks, that's changed. And now I think it's important for us to be prepared in case things escalate quickly," he said.
Under the executive order, a group of experts will be tasked with creating safety guidelines for AI systems within two months.
"California wants to create the standards in this space," Newsom said.
The governor said the effort will include developing oversight measures such as independent reviews and audits of AI systems. The order also calls for planning around potential emergency responses.
"Advancing efforts to create an emergency shut off, otherwise known as an AI kill switch, which means a lot of things depending on who you talk to. So we want to flesh out exactly what that means," Newsom said.
Yashas Hariprasad, an assistant professor at Cal State East Bay, compared the current state of AI to a young dog that still requires supervision and training.
"Sometimes a puppy can go rogue, and it might not be to hurt a human, being intentionally, but sometimes it's just growing its teeth, and it tries to nibble on something," Hariprasad said.
He said safety guidelines are needed to ensure AI systems remain beneficial to people.
"We want to make sure that AI is helping us. And AI is here to serve humans. So, we want to protect humans. And in order to do that, we need to build security across AI systems," Hariprasad said.
While California is moving forward with its own framework, some experts said broader action will ultimately be necessary.
"We do need to take this seriously as a country, because if you do it in one state, it could move to another state. So yeah, national and actually global action is actually what we need," Goldberg said.
The next phase of the effort could involve AI safety laws at the national level. Newsom has said he would like Congress to adopt similar approaches.
ABC7 Eyewitness News Reporter Dryden Quigley contributed to this report.
CNN's Hadas Gold contributed to this report.

Title: Historic "base ball" national championship comes to Sussex County
Article_Text:
LEWES, Del. - Baseball will look a little different at Hudson Fields this weekend.
There will be no fielding gloves, no running through first base and no modern uniforms. Instead, teams from across the region and country will compete for a national championship while playing the game as it was played in 1864.
The Lewes Base Ball Club is hosting the 2026 National Association of Historic Base Ball Clubs National Championship on Saturday and Sunday, bringing historic base ball clubs to coastal Delaware for a weekend of competition and a trip back in time.
Mike “Oyster” DiPaolo, president and captain of the Lewes club, said the team has wanted to host an event of this size for some time.
“We’ve been wanting to do an event like this for a while,” DiPaolo said. “We were really excited because we think this is a beautiful place to play baseball, and it’s a great place to visit.”
DiPaolo said teams are making the trip from states including Rhode Island, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland. For some, he said, it will be their first visit to coastal Delaware.
Once they take the field, the game will be recognizable, but several rules will stand out to modern baseball fans.
Players do not use fielding gloves. A ball caught on one bounce can still record an out, runners cannot overrun first base and there is no traditional home run fence. Foul balls can also affect base runners differently than they do in today’s game.
“Well, it’s going to look like baseball. It’s going to feel like baseball. It’s going to sound like baseball, but you’re going to see some differences,” DiPaolo said.
Pitching is also done underhand, although DiPaolo said pitchers can still put plenty of speed and movement on the ball.
The uniforms and language are designed to add to the experience. Players use period-style clothing, umpires are known as arbiters and many players take on colorful nicknames.
John “Cheese” Chisholm has played historic base ball for about a decade and now competes with two clubs. He said the history surrounding the game is what keeps him coming back.
“When you’re out there on the field and you see people showing up wearing period costumes and outfits, and the umpires dressed in a top hat and coat and so forth, it’s just the history of it,” Chisholm said. “I’m doing something that people were doing back in 1864.”
Alex “Haybale” Langley joined the Lewes club in 2023 after years of playing slow-pitch softball. He said playing without a glove was one of the biggest adjustments.
“You begin to adapt,” Langley said. “It’s enough difference to be sort of fun and quirky without being too challenging.”
Despite the vintage appearance, players said the competition will be serious once the national championship begins.
DiPaolo said teams still play hard and want to win, even if the atmosphere remains friendly.
“It’s competitive. People want to win,” DiPaolo said. “No one’s holding back, but no one’s going in spikes up either.”
For the Lewes players, hosting the championship is also an opportunity to showcase both the sport and the area to visitors who may have never seen historic base ball before.
And while plenty has changed in the game over the past 162 years, DiPaolo said at least one baseball rule still stands.
“There’s no crying in baseball.”

Title: Kingston zoning board approves Jewish girls school
Article_Text:
KINGSTON — A new Jewish girls school is a step closer to opening and residents are celebrating what they say a victory for education and community.
The Kingston Zoning Hearing Board determined Wednesday that a property at 230 Pringle Street could be used as a school by the Jewish education group Cheder Menachem. Its decision, which is subject to a 30-day appeal period, came after the municipality entered into a federal consent decree to amend zoning regulations that the U.S. Department of Justice alleged encroached upon residents’ religious freedoms.
Cheder Menachem School Director Yosef Baumgarten said the new building on Pringle Street was needed to accommodate a rapidly expanding student body, which has grown from around 150 students several years ago to nearly 700 now.
“I’m very excited and happy that we were approved,” Baumgarten said after the meeting. “It’s very much needed for the school, as well as for the community as it grows.”
The Pringle Street property in question is located in an R3 residential zone. It has most recently been used as a plumbing and heating business and the zoning board is authorizing its use as a school now by way of special exception.
The new Cheder Menachem school is to host female students from sixth through 12th grade. It will join a Cheder Menachem boys school for kindergarten through eighth grade located at the former Schuyler Avenue school purchased from Wyoming Valley West; and a pre-kindergarten through fifth-grade boys school located at the former Coughlin High School in Wilkes-Barre.
Baumgarten, speaking to the zoning board, noted the Pringle Street property, before becoming a storefront for a plumbing business, the building previously served as a school.
“So, although we are applying for a special exception to change it, it’s actually bringing it back,” Baumgarten said. “We’re really bringing it back to its former glory, its former use.”
Several residents joined Baumgarten in speaking at the hearing, with all testifying in favor of the school.
Dina Aizenman, an educator with Cheder Menachem and the head of its middle school division, also testified. She said she was looking forward to working with municipal officials in building that stronger education environment.
“I am here today as a mother for three girls that still lack a proper space for their schooling, but also as an educator,” Aizenman said. “I believe that everything that we can do must be done for the benefit of those young women, so they can grow to become fine, well educated adults true to their heritage.”
Noa Barak, a Cheder Menachem high school student, also spoke in favor of Cheder Menachem. She said she was eager to have a home school building that she and her classmates could call their own.
“In the past, the girls in attendance at the school, haven’t really had a permanent building,” Barak said. “And this year we want to change that, we want to feel more at home in our school.”
Barak also thanked Cheder Menachem for creating a family atmosphere around the school and said she believed the new school building would help create a strong, community-wide sense of belonging.
“In addition, we want to have motivation and solidify ourselves in the school and growing community,” Barak said.
Richard Michalowsky said the Jewish community supporting the school was eager to partner with its neighbors throughout the municipality. He reflected on the message of community partnership in the context of the holiday Rosh Hashanah, a Jewish holiday celebrating the new year which began the evening of Sept. 11 and ended Sunday.
“We pray for a good year, not only for ourselves, but for the world at large,” Michalowsky said. “We should all be blessed, the community of Kingston, the United States of America, and the world at large, with a good, sweet and prosperous year.”
The special exception granted to Cheder Menachem follows what has been a monthslong process that began with a federal civil rights investigation.
On Feb. 4, the U.S. Department of Justice sued Kingston over alleged violation of the Religious Land Use And Institutionalized Persons Act, federal legislation prohibiting religiously discriminatory municipal zoning. The suit targeted a 2023 zoning ordinance that categorically barred places of worship from opening in residential zones; and required those opening in commercial zones to obtain a special exception and operate on parcels of at least 1 acre. Similar restrictions were generally not placed on non-religious sites.
This disparity, the federal lawsuit argued, would have an especially burdensome effect on Kingston’s burgeoning Chabad Orthodox Jewish community. As part of its case, the Justice Department cited Kingston’s zoning restrictions on opening new schools, which it said precluded the much needed expansion of Cheder Menachem for the municipality’s growing number of Chabad Orthodox Jewish children.
Kingston, while not admitting it had violated RLUIPA, entered into a federal consent decree with the Justice Department the same day the suit was filed. Under the consent decree, the municipality promised to amend its zoning ordinance to better accommodate religious institutions, which it did July 7. Among the amendments added was a provision allowing religious schools to operate in residential zones by special exception.
Alex Brunelle, an attorney who spoke on behalf of Cheder Menachem on Wednesday and who has also represented another Jewish organization involved in other RLIUPA litigation, said he was encouraged by the zoning hearing Wednesday.
“I’m happy to be here on a much happier note than some prior meetings I’ve had to attend involving Kingston, Pennsylvania,” Brunelle said. “I feel that Kingston’s really trying to embrace the community and turn over, frankly, a new leaf on making things shared and collaborative….”
Neighbors of the planned school struck a similarly optimistic tone.
“A whole bunch of my neighbors go to the school and they’re just delightful kids,” resident Kris Luminar said. “And I think it’s nice to see new life being breathed into an old building and it’s back to being what it’s supposed to be, a school for children.”
Nexhat Imeraj, an Albanian man who has invested in a nearby property, also spoke in support of the school. He said he received the municipality’s letter to neighbors notifying him about the meeting and that he wanted to come to express support.
“I got the letter for tonight and I saw how they want to change the direction from planning to school,” Imeraj said. “I come to tell you…they have my vote…and I’m glad I’m going to be their neighbor.”

Title: Griezmann hurt, status unknown for Orlando City against New England
Article_Text:
Orlando City looks to continue its hot streak in Major League Soccer play when the Lions visit the New England Revolution on Saturday night.
Orlando City, though, will likely face New England without injured star Antoine Griezmann. Griezmann left the Lions’ 2-1 loss to Columbus in a semifinal of U.S. Open Cup on Wednesday. Griezmann was forced out of the match in the second half and did not train with the team Friday.
The Lions (10-11-4, 34 points) will try for their fourth consecutive MLS win and run their unbeaten streak to six matches when they take on the Revolution (13-8-4, 43 points) at Gillette Stadium at 7:30 p.m. Orlando City is sixth in the Eastern Conference. New England is third.
“We just have to flip the page,” said Orlando City forward Justin Ellis. “Obviously, we were pretty sad about the Columbus game. I feel we could have played a lot better. We didn’t really play at our best level, but we have to flip the page. We have a tough game (Saturday), and we have to get three points.”
Ellis has been instrumental to Orlando’s climb up the table as the Lions have reversed their fortunes after a 1-5 start to the campaign. He has three goals and 11 assists in his breakthrough season. The 19-year-old also earned his first call-up to the U.S. Men’s National Team.
His potential debut with the USMNT could come next Saturday at Inter.co Stadium when the Americans face off against Peru in a friendly. For now, however, his primary focus is on helping Orlando City beat New England.
“It’s about just staying in the present, staying in the moment,” Ellis said. “I feel like that’s what I do a good job of, and just try and help the team win tomorrow, and then, after tomorrow, I can put my focus into the national team.”
Ellis will be even more important Saturday with the expected absence of Griezmann. If Griezmann is unable to play, Ellis and Martín Ojeda (11 goals and an assist) will lead the attack against a stout New England defense that has only allowed 31 goals in 25 games.
The good news for Orlando is that New England has won only two of its last six home games this season. The Revolution will also be without the injured duo of Jack Harrison and Alhassan Yusuf. They still boast plenty of attacking talent in the likes of Carles Gil (10 goals, four assists) and Dor Turgeman (seven goals, five assists).
Additional, Matt Turner has been one of the best goalkeepers in MLS this season and ranks fourth, just ahead of Orlando City’s Maxime Crepeau, in saves, with 98 to Crepeau’s 96.
The Revolution had two players called up to the national team: midfielder Brooklyn Raines and defender Peyton Miller.
The sixth-place Lions need a win to stay securely in a playoff spot, as they are only four points clear of Red Bull New York in 10th. The gap between sixth and 12th is only five points, so there is little room for error with only nine league games remaining.
Orlando’s next match is on the road against the Philadelphia Union and 16-year-old sensation Cavan Sullivan on Sept. 26.

Title: Dallas Cowboys: Washington Commanders have been 'get right' opponent before
Article_Text:
The 2026 Dallas Cowboys were supposed to find themselves in better positions to compete in all phases compared to the 7-9-1 campaign of a year ago. Instead, after one game, they find themselves in eerily similar position ahead of a week two divisional game at home.
Commanders have been ‘get right’ opponent for Cowboys before
The Cowboys and Commanders each desperately need a win.
Last season began with a primetime road loss by one score to a NFC East rival, putting the Cowboys in a bit of a “prove it or lose it” spot back in their home stadium against another division opponent, the Giants, in week two. The Cowboys won that game ugly in overtime, and it felt ominous for how this team would play against better competition.
If things were at least slightly optimistic following last year’s close week one loss to the reigning Super Bowl champions, this week has been a category five hurricane that has fans ready to jump ship if the Cowboys do anything less than beat the Commanders handily. Yes, a Commanders team that was just within a few plays of beating the Eagles on the road in their first outing.
Luckily, the Cowboys have used recent games against the Commanders in this way before, as Sunday will be the fifth time they go up against their former defensive coordinator Dan Quinn since he became the Commanders’ head coach in 2024.
Dallas is 3-1 in these games scoring at least 30 points in each win, and the one loss was Week 18 of 2024 when Trey Lance started for Dak Prescott. That game was also the Commanders’ first win in Arlington since Thanksgiving of 2020.
Last season, the Cowboys came into the home game against the Commanders off a deflating, one-score road loss to the Panthers. The defense was bad, wasn’t even put in position to succeed if they wanted to in critical moments of the game, and the offense made costly mistakes. Sound familiar?
The Cowboys responded with a 44-22 win against the Commanders, a season high for points. Dak Prescott had his second highest yards per attempt of the season, completed 70% of his passes, and threw two touchdowns to Jake Ferguson plus another to CeeDee Lamb. The approach on offense was balanced with 31 rushing attempts, 19 from Javonte Williams for 116 yards and a touchdown, and 30 pass attempts for Prescott.
The Cowboys got points on drives that started at their own 34 yard line to start the game, own 40, 46, 45, and 33 to win the battle of field position. As a season long trend the Cowboys were very poor in this area, and that was among the long list of concerns after last week’s Giants game for the current Cowboys too, but taking the ball away from the Commanders twice while also making two stops on fourth downs went a long way.
The Cowboys will know what they’re seeing in the Dan Quinn defense, one that remained aggressive but had it’s struggles in week one against the Eagles. After failing to establish Ferguson as a threat against the Giants defense, the Cowboys should be encouraged by Eagles tight end Dallas Goedert leading Philly in catches and yards with two touchdowns last Sunday. Both touchdowns came from distance too, one of 17 yards and the other 43.
In the Commanders secondary that will look to be the second straight to keep George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb in check, Nick Cross, Amik Robertson, and Mike Sainristill were all at the top of the Commanders box score for tackles against the Eagles. This is normally not a good sign of how well a defense won at the point of attack, and also points to something else that will be familiar for Cowboys fans and coaches alike for this matchup against Quinn, which is defensive backs on an island.
In an eight point loss in week one, the Cowboys lost an expected 8.3 points to three costly drops. All of the ingredients are in place for the Cowboys to get all of their skill players involved in the game plan this week, calm down the fan base by getting push in the run game, spreading it around through the air, and flipping the script the Giants used on them by having their own offense control a home game.
The other win for the Cowboys against the Commanders last year came on Christmas Day. This time around they were coming in off a season-worst three-game losing streak. A Week 14 Thursday night loss at the Lions felt like the official end to vague playoff hopes, but another primetime loss the following week at home to the Vikings followed by a no-show type performance and loss to the Chargers had the feeling around Christmas anything but jolly. Dallas had already played on Thanksgiving and beaten the Chiefs, but there was little reason to expect more holiday cheer in this game.
The Cowboys caught a break with the Commanders having an injury at quarterback, something that’s been a theme of this rivalry as of late, starting veteran journeyman Josh Johnson. Washington went 1-6 on third down and 1-3 scoring touchdowns in the red zone, seeing Dallas come in and win 30-23. KaVontae Turpin scored an 86-yard touchdown down the middle of the field in the second quarter to push the Cowboys lead to 21-3.
This upcoming game should be an opportunity for Christian Parker’s defense and the Cowboys to keep the ball in front of them, play downhill at linebacker, and win their matchups on the outside. Anything short of this with the Commanders offense picking up where the Giants left off in confusing and physically outperforming the Cowboys defense would be a serious letdown.
If there’s a very general, overall takeaway from week one in the books around the NFL, it’s that coaching is at an all-time importance in games being decided by a razor’s margin. We already said that this week has been toxic around the Cowboys fanbase, but it hasn’t quite reached outcries for the likes of Schottenheimer, Parker, or other coaches to lose their jobs. The same can’t be said for Quinn in Washington who has had the feel of outstaying his welcome for a little bit now within that fanbase, and this also needs to be an area the Cowboys win the Xs and Os battle this week to preserve the optimism of this season.
Speaking of, the last time the Cowboys started 0-2 was 2010, which was also the last time they made an in-season coaching change from Wade Phillips to Jason Garrett. Even that year’s Cowboys team beat Washington at home for win number five of six that season.
The Cowboys have not started a season 0-2 with both losses coming against division opponents since 2000, the second to last year of the Cardinals being in the East. Dallas lost at home to Philadelphia in week one and in Arizona week two. That Dave Campo led Cowboys team finished with even fewer wins than 2010 with five, and even they had two against Washington.
The Cowboys need this game in the worst way in their first appearance on America’s Game of the Week on FOX.

Title: 22 regional data center projects and where they stand
Article_Text:
The developer of at least one of the 22 data center campuses proposed for Northeastern Pennsylvania doesn’t expect the executive order Gov. Josh Shapiro signed in August to slow down the project.
The Nebius AI cloud campus project in Butler Twp., Schuylkill County, is on track, John Sutter, vice president of U.S. Public Affairs at Nebius, said in a written statement in response to an inquiry.
“(We) are committed to developing data centers responsibly and in close coordination with local communities — an approach consistent with the executive order’s focus on responsible development and local engagement,” Sutter said.
Shapiro’s Aug. 18 order, which contains safeguards he has touted as “the strictest guardrails in the nation” for data centers, requires developers to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) Requirements or risk losing a 6% state sales tax exemption.
The order removes all current and future data centers from the PA Permit Fast Track program designed to streamline and accelerate state government permitting for high-impact economic development and infrastructure projects and requires developers to secure all local approvals before the state will even begin to review permit applications.
Operators must invest in local economies, create jobs and negotiate community benefit agreements, as well.
The newspaper reached out to eight developers or their attorneys behind 12 data center campus projects in Lackawanna, Luzerne and Schuylkill counties to ask how the executive order would affect project timelines, if at all, and only Nebius and one other developer responded.
An Amazon spokesperson didn’t directly answer the question for its projects in Hazle and Salem townships in Luzerne County and in Kline Twp. in Schuylkill County, but the spokesperson did indicate that the company was complying with at least one directive in the executive order – job creation.
“In 2025, Amazon made a deep commitment to Pennsylvania – a $20 billion planned data center investment that’s expected to create at least 1,250 new high-skilled jobs while supporting thousands of other jobs in the data center supply chain in the Commonwealth,” the spokesperson said.
“This builds on our existing footprint of more than 31,000 full- and part-time employees and an economic presence that supports over 20,000 additional jobs across industries like construction, logistics, and professional services. We’re committed to being good neighbors in the communities where we build and operate, and will continue working with state and local leaders to invest responsibly and create good jobs,” the spokesperson concluded.
Nebius’ Sutter promised local cooperation and community involvement, as well.
“We’re grateful for early support from Butler Township leaders and we will continue working closely with community members and state officials throughout the development process,” Sutter said.

Title: Researchers Say They've Found the Truth About Thomas Jefferson
Article_Text:
Researchers Say They’ve Found the Truth About Thomas Jefferson
A secret 15-year effort has produced genetic evidence that one of the nation’s Founders fathered children with a woman he enslaved.
Three hours after Thomas Jefferson died at his Monticello home on July 4, 1826, his personal secretary, Nicholas Trist, snipped a lock of the Founder’s gray hair, still faintly reddish blond. Trist then tied the hair with orange thread and placed it in a paper packet, along with a short note describing what he’d done.
In an era before photography or modern embalming, hair was an easily preserved reminder of a beloved friend or relative who’d died. Trist did not know that he was also securing physical evidence that, two centuries later, would help resolve one of the nation’s oldest and most contentious historical debates: whether the author of the Declaration of Independence, the nation’s third president, had children with Sally Hemings, a woman he enslaved for half a century and never freed.
After a covert and exhaustive 15-year effort led by the Smithsonian Institution, a team of geneticists, genealogists, historians, and anthropologists believe it has found proof that Jefferson fathered at least two of Hemings’s six children. On Tuesday, Richard Kurin, a Smithsonian cultural anthropologist, who led the multidisciplinary research effort, will publish a book detailing the team’s findings. A scientific paper is currently under review for publication in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The researchers, who agreed to speak with me about their results before publication, relied on the latest genetic techniques to reassemble Jefferson’s genome from the Founder’s hair. They then matched that sequence with DNA from descendants of two of Hemings’s sons, Madison and Eston. (Of her other four children, two died in infancy, and the other two didn’t have any known offspring.) Not only did the researchers find that Madison’s and Eston’s descendants share Jefferson’s DNA; many of them had more of it than do his known descendants by way of his wife, Martha Wayles.
For many Americans, the matter was already laid to rest years ago. In 1998, the scientific journal Nature published a two-page peer-reviewed paper titled “Jefferson Fathered Slave’s Last Child.” Newspaper stories declared the case solved, and Oprah Winfrey staged a tearful family reunion of Jefferson’s descendants. Most historians came to accept the finding when it was combined with other evidence from the era.
But a vocal minority has continued to doubt that the two had a sexual relationship. Some have pointed out, correctly, that the limited biological data used in the Nature study did not definitively prove that Jefferson was the father of Hemings’s children—only that he was one of several candidates in the Jefferson male line. These doubters also disparage as unreliable or wishful thinking the oral histories passed down by Hemings’s descendants who have placed Jefferson in their family tree.
Some detractors saw a more nefarious agenda. One researcher called the 1998 study “a deliberate attempt to select and mold the evidence to fit a pre-selected theory.” Other critics, many of them white Virginians, joined in the defense of the Founder. “Jefferson’s personal reputation has been all but assassinated,” wrote William G. Hyland Jr., a lawyer and author. “The face on Mount Rushmore has been vilified as a slave-owning hypocrite, misogynist, and racist.”
Though the new results might convince some holdouts, the backlash has already arrived, and more will likely follow. The Heritage Foundation has previously criticized Monticello’s depiction of Jefferson in part for failing to tell visitors “that historians disagree about Jefferson’s relationship with Sally Hemings.” The Thomas Jefferson Heritage Society, a nonprofit formed in response to the Nature report, still accuses “historical revisionists” of inaccurately portraying Jefferson as a “liar, fraud, hypocrite, and child molesting slave rapist.” The Trump administration has made clear that it wants to present a version of American history that doesn’t disparage the Founders. In a report released on the Fourth of July, the White House condemned what it asserted is “extreme political activism” guiding the 180-year-old Smithsonian, which President Trump has said is too focused on “how bad Slavery was.”
For Clara Nutt, though, the results are simply confirmation of a long-known fact. Her African American father told his freckled daughter at an early age that she was a direct descendant of Jefferson through Madison Hemings. Nutt provided the researchers with saliva samples that found 5.1 percent of Jefferson’s genetic makeup in her DNA—nearly twice the amount expected by genetic averaging. She was delighted but not surprised to have scientific proof. “I have always known who I am,” Nutt told me.
That the very person who made famous the phrase “All men are created equal” repeatedly impregnated a woman he held in lifetime bondage first surfaced in a Richmond newspaper in 1802. The writer, a Scottish-born journalist named James Callender, had once been a Jefferson champion, and had received financial support from him. But when Jefferson won the 1800 election, he denied a government job to the volatile Callender, who had been jailed during John Adams’s administration for sedition. Ally turned enemy. “By this wench Sally, our president has had several children,” Callender wrote in The Recorder. “The AFRICAN VENUS is said to officiate, as housekeeper at Monticello.”
The Hemings-Jefferson matter became one of the nation’s first major political scandals—and one of its most enduring. “This engaged six of the seven first presidents,” Richard Kurin told me. “You could call it the longest-running American soap opera”—one, he notes, that involves the issues of race, inequality, and liberty.
Jefferson, after all, declared in 1814 that “amalgamation with the other color produces a degradation to which no lover of his country, no lover of excellence in the human character can innocently consent.” By that date, his youngest child with Hemings, Eston, was 6 years old. Jefferson’s granddaughter Ellen Randolph Coolidge, in an 1858 letter to her husband, referred to the possibility of a relationship with Hemings as that which “will not bear telling. There are such things, after all, as moral impossibilities.” The Founder went to his grave without publicly acknowledging the relationship or any children he’d had with Hemings.
A 1974 book by the historian Fawn Brodie reignited the debate with fresh historical evidence of Jefferson’s long-term liaison with Hemings, but Brodie’s assertions gained little traction among scholars and intellectuals. If the Hemings story was true, one skeptical historian wrote in 1977, then Jefferson “deserves to be regarded as one of the most profligate liars and consummate hypocrites ever to occupy the presidency.” Gore Vidal summarized the prevailing sentiment in an interview: “No gentleman would have gone to bed with a slave. Since Thomas Jefferson was the greatest gentleman of his period, he could not have done so either. That takes care of that.”
Two decades later, the Harvard law professor Annette Gordon-Reed sharply criticized the academic community for spending “generations either ignoring or explaining away” the nearly four-decade relationship and accepting white narratives denying the tie while dismissing those left by Black families that asserted otherwise.
The 1998 Nature report brought the new tools of genetics to bear on the dispute. The authors based their biological data on the Y chromosome, passed down by Jefferson’s male descendants. But some researchers accused the authors of misleading the public, and the authors were forced to acknowledge that Jefferson could “neither be definitively excluded nor solely implicated” by their data. Other candidates included his younger brother, Randolph, a frequent visitor to Monticello. One enslaved informant had called Randolph “a mighty simple man” who “used to come out among black people, play the fiddle & dance half the night.”
A month after the Nature study’s publication, the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, which owns and operates Monticello, convened a group of scholars to examine the genetic and historical data. A 2000 statistical analysis by a Monticello archaeologist strengthened the case made in Nature by examining the timing of when Jefferson was present at Monticello and when Hemings’s children were conceived. A majority of the foundation’s panel found “a high probability” that at least one of Hemings’s children had been fathered by Jefferson, and likely all six. A minority, however, rejected the conclusions, calling the research a cynical campaign by academics and the media “to denigrate and destroy the legacy of one of the greatest of our founding fathers and one of the greatest of all our citizens.”
Critics united to form the Thomas Jefferson Heritage Society, which undertook a second independent review of the findings in the Nature study, and declared the Thomas Jefferson Foundation’s report “the product of shallow and shoddy scholarship” that had ignored exculpatory evidence “in order to achieve an apparently desired conclusion.” John Works, a Jefferson descendant and founding member of the society, wrote that defending the author of the Declaration “has come to mean defending what America means, and we feel compelled to rise to that defense.” The report that the society’s panel of scholars released in 2001 found the Nature results “almost certainly false,” and insisted that “Sally Hemings appears to have been a very minor figure in Thomas Jefferson’s life.”
The controversy spawned books with subtitles such as An American Travesty, and Fallacies, Omissions, and Contradictions in the Hemings Genealogical Search, which expanded on critiques of the genetic study and the historical data. “Jefferson is completely innocent of this sordid charge,” William Hyland maintained in his book In Defense of Thomas Jefferson, citing “an obsessive agenda on the color of Sally’s skin, and slave status.” Another doubter, David N. Mayer, a law and history professor in Ohio, fingered “‘political correctness,’ radical multiculturalism, and postmodernism.”
Hemings was born in 1773 as the youngest child of the enslaved Elizabeth Hemings, described by one enslaved man at Monticello as “a bright mulatto woman.” Sally, he recalled, was “mighty near white” and “very handsome; long straight hair down her back.” One of Jefferson’s grandsons described her as “light colored and decidedly good looking.” Both enslaved and free contemporaries reported that her father was John Wayles, the father of Jefferson’s wife, Martha. If true, then Hemings was Martha’s half sister.
On her deathbed in 1782, Martha is said to have made her husband promise not to remarry. Five years later, he was in Paris serving as the minister plenipotentiary when his daughter Maria arrived, accompanied by the 14-year-old Hemings. Madison Hemings later claimed that Jefferson and his mother began a sexual relationship while in France, where she was legally free, and that she agreed to return to the United States on the condition that any future children would be freed at age 21.
In an interview with a journalist, Madison stated that his mother was pregnant by Jefferson on their return to the United States in 1789, though it is unclear whether any child from that time survived. Hemings went on to serve in the main house of Monticello while her owner joined George Washington’s Cabinet as the nation’s first secretary of state, and then became president from 1801 to 1809. As he did with all of his human property, Jefferson recorded the birth of Hemings’s six children, including a son, Beverly, in 1798; a daughter, Harriet, in 1801; a son, Madison, in 1805; and another son, Eston, in 1808. Two other daughters, one born in 1797 and another in 1799, died in infancy. The three sons trained as carpenters, and Harriet spun and wove cloth.
Both Beverly and Harriet fled Monticello in 1822. Jefferson, who often posted rewards or hired slave catchers to return those who escaped, did not attempt to recover either. By Madison Hemings’s account, Beverly went to Washington, D.C., passed as white, and married a white woman. Monticello’s former chief overseer later claimed that Jefferson had arranged for Harriet’s departure, giving her spending money and stage-coach fare to Philadelphia. She “married a white man in good standing” in the capital, Madison recalled in his later years.
In Jefferson’s will, made out months before his 1826 death, he granted Madison and Eston Hemings their freedom once they reached 21, and gave both men “my last, solemn, and dutiful thanks.” He also asked the Virginia government—which required those emancipated to leave the state—to allow the Hemings brothers to remain “where their families and connections are.” Sally Hemings was never officially freed, although Jefferson’s daughter Martha later let Sally live with the freed Madison and Eston in Charlottesville until her death, in 1835. Her burial location, like that of so many enslaved African Americans, is unknown.
Both Madison and Eston later moved to Ohio. Eston died in 1856 in Wisconsin. His two sons fought for the Union in the Civil War, and the family obscured its African American heritage. “We identified as white,” Arthur Westerinen, Eston’s fifth-generation descendant, told me. Westerinen’s mother, Julia, learned of the connection when she stumbled on it while doing a college ancestry project.
Madison’s branch, however, retained its African American identity and passed down the story of Jefferson’s paternity. When a teenage Clara Nutt visited Monticello on a school trip in the early 1970s, she was eager to see the home of her famous ancestors. “I got off the bus with my head held high,” she recalled. Shown Jefferson’s bedroom, she asked a docent where Sally Hemings had slept. “That woman never stepped foot in this house,” the docent snapped. Nutt was devastated. “With every breath,” she said, “I silently sobbed.”
In his new book, History by a Hair, the Smithsonian’s Kurin tells the story of how he and his fellow researchers tracked down Jefferson’s DNA. In October 2011, Kurin was reviewing a film to accompany a Smithsonian exhibit displaying what is known as The Jefferson Bible. After retiring to Monticello, Jefferson compiled the volume by painstakingly cutting and pasting sections of the New Testament that were focused on morality and stripped of what he called the “artificial vestments” of miracles and superstitions. The film included a segment featuring a reenactor working with a sharp penknife under candlelight. Kurin, then the Smithsonian’s secretary for history, art, and culture, mused to himself that if he had taken on such a delicate task, he would have repeatedly cut himself. That idle thought prompted him to contact a curator who had worked on the bible’s conservation to see if he had encountered any blood splotches that might contain Jefferson’s DNA.
The curator told Kurin that he had found no blood but had encountered a couple of hairs. One was pasted down on page 73 and was light red, like Jefferson’s hair. At the time, extracting DNA from old hair was cutting-edge science; light and humidity can quickly degrade genetic material. Only in the previous year had a Danish team succeeded in sequencing an ancient genome using a clump of 4,000-year-old human hair that had been well preserved in the ice of Greenland.
With approval from Smithsonian leaders, Kurin launched an investigation to reconstruct Jefferson’s genome using the hair found in the bible, while also gathering saliva samples from dozens of living individuals who were known or suspected descendants. By comparing the first with the second, he hoped to produce unequivocal evidence of the paternity of Hemings’s children.
From the start, the ambitious effort was kept secret from the public. “We didn’t want people to assume results until we were really, really sure,” Kurin told me. A colleague of his reached out to a couple in the genetics field, the molecular biologist Beth Shapiro and her husband, Richard Green, a computational expert who had made a name sequencing the Neanderthal genome. They were starting a paleogenomics lab at UC Santa Cruz. “We knew the technology was getting better,” Shapiro told me. “And this looked cool, interesting, and fun.”
Years into the project, Shapiro and Green’s lab determined that the bible hairs had not, in fact, belonged to Jefferson. A reliquary at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, purporting to contain hair from the first 14 presidents, also proved a dead end. “I thought that was it,” Shapiro said. Kurin, however, had already begun to scour other collections. Monticello’s storage areas yielded several samples of Jefferson’s hair encased in gold lockets, glass ampules, and the packet assembled by Nicholas Trist. Kurin also found additional corroboration of the latter’s validity: In 1899, Trist’s daughter had mailed the packet to her cousin, writing that the hair was “in the same paper in which they were placed on that day nearly 74 years ago,” and which “I know to be authentic.”
With the permission of the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, the geneticists examined the hair strands and found viable DNA. “We’ll exhaust it and sequence the crap out of it,” Shapiro assured Kurin in 2017. Lab workers gradually assembled a library of Jefferson’s genome. “We went from a long-shot fishing expedition to a slam dunk,” Green said. “From then on, it was pretty straightforward. We spend a lot of time getting DNA out of difficult things like hair.” (Many of the lab’s recent projects have centered on identifying victims and suspects in cold cases, including the Gilgo Beach murders.)
Kurin, meanwhile, traveled the country to meet with known and possible Hemings-Jefferson descendants, including Julia Westerinen and Nutt. He explained his mission, gained consent, collected saliva samples, and secured promises that they would keep the matter private. This second library of material allowed the geneticists to compare the DNA from descendants of Madison and Eston Hemings with DNA from Jefferson.
The match proved indisputable. On average, a fifth-generation descendant retains 3.125 percent of their ancestor’s genetic material, though the precise amount can vary considerably. Two fifth-generation descendants of Jefferson and Martha Wayles showed 2.6 percent and 2.7 percent of Jefferson’s genetic material. Nutt’s percentage was nearly twice that. Other Madison relations shared significant amounts of the third president’s DNA, as did descendants of Eston. The scientists had found their proof, thanks to Jefferson’s hair. “Once you have a common ancestor,” Green said, “the accuracy is absolutely stunning.”
The research effort has begun to face criticism even before it is publicly released. One descendant of Madison Hemings, Mary Brady-Atkins, provided DNA samples for the study, but criticized Kurin this week in an interview in The Chronicle of Higher Education. Brady-Atkins said she was concerned that Kurin’s book would be published before the scientific paper.
Last month, the 98-year-old Brady-Atkins asked that her saliva samples be destroyed. “It was her right to withdraw from the study,” Kurin told me today. “And yes, we destroyed her DNA, and withdrew data from the study, but the findings are still the same.” He acknowledged that the book would come out before PNAS has accepted the paper, and noted that Brady-Atkins’s request to be removed from the project came after the book was already printed. But Kurin and Green insisted that the study was undergoing appropriate peer review. Green added that a draft of the paper with detailed data will be released on Tuesday, at the same time as the book.
According to the Chronicle, Brady-Atkins supports a competing research effort led by Works, the Jefferson descendant who helped found the Heritage Society; he has long argued that Randolph Jefferson, rather than his brother Thomas, was the father of Hemings’s children. Last year, Works petitioned a county court in Tennessee to exhume the body of Randolph’s son from a Nashville cemetery, with the goal of extracting DNA that Works believes might clear Thomas Jefferson’s name. The city opposes the petition.
Some descendants worry that the new research from Kurin and his colleagues will only infuriate die-hard Jefferson apologists further. “It will be ugly,” Nutt predicted. Unlike during her first Monticello visit, however, she now feels supported. After the Nature paper came out, she attended a reunion of her late father’s family and was drawn into the community of Hemings’s descendants. In 2001, she participated in a White House event hosted by President George W. Bush that brought together Jefferson’s progeny on both sides of the color line. “Whatever comes, I can lean into my family—and my new family,” she said, including the researchers who gathered the hard data confirming her family’s ties.
One likely flash point will be the policies of the Monticello Association, a private organization that oversees the Jefferson-family cemetery at Monticello. The group has long refused to allow Hemings’s descendants to join the association, much less be buried alongside their white relations. “They are invested in this idea of Thomas Jefferson on a pedestal,” Arthur Westerinen said. He told me that he has been in contact with several association members who have pressed for the acceptance of the Hemings branch of the family, though without success. (Lucy Taylor, the association’s president, did not respond to requests for comment.)
Another “giant question,” Green said, is what becomes of Jefferson’s genome. According to Green, two major National Institutes of Health–funded genetic-data banks recently rejected the team’s request to submit its detailed sequence. This is in part because Jefferson is a known figure; if Jefferson’s genome is made public, then his descendants’ privacy will be at risk. “The descendant community will need to weigh in,” Green said. “My lab worked hard on this, but I don’t want to be the one who decides who gets access.”
At the same time, the data, were they publicly released, could allow individuals to determine their own relation to the third president—and, perhaps, pinpoint descendants of Beverly and Harriet Hemings to see if they, too, were born of the Hemings-Jefferson relationship. By recovering the genome of Jefferson’s wife, Martha, researchers also could confirm whether she is Sally Hemings’s half sister.
More broadly, the UC Santa Cruz team’s success might spark a rush to recover the genomes of other famous people—Beethoven’s, for example, was recently sequenced from locks of his hair. Such an effort would have intriguing but unsettling implications. “You could search to see if Abraham Lincoln’s melancholy was genetic,” Kurin suggested. Green fears that rapid technological advances might lead to a genetic Wild West. “Genes are not necessarily fate; most simply create a predisposition,” he said. He worries that members of the media will fail to convey this complexity, much as the 1998 Nature headline was misleading. He also fears a backlash that might result in unreasonable barriers to research.
When it comes to Jefferson and Hemings, Kurin is confident that the team’s careful work over a decade and a half will convince doubters of the accuracy of their finding. “For me, it had nothing to do with an ideological or political agenda,” he writes in his new book. “I was using evidence, logic, and the available tools and methods to follow a trail.” He also takes Jefferson at his word. “There is not a truth existing which I fear,” the Founder wrote two months before his death, “or would wish unknown to the whole world.”

Title: Philadelphia 'House of Horrors' linked to 7 missing women, cops recover over 1 million digital files
Article_Text:
Philadelphia 'House of Horrors' linked to 7 missing women, cops recover over 1 million digital files
The investigation into what is being called the "House of Horror" continues in Philadelphia after more than 1 million individual digital items — including images, videos and writings — have been recovered from a home linked to Eugene Horsch and his late father, Raymond "R.C." Horsch, as part of a large ongoing case involving several missing women.
Authorities say they are reviewing more than 600,000 images, 70,000 videos and 10,000 pages of writing from the property. Police also recovered guns, gun parts, drugs, chemicals and other evidence. The investigation at the home led to the excavation of the property and the discovery of urns containing cremated remains.
7 missing women linked to investigation
What we know:
Philadelphia police have linked seven missing women to the property, according to police sources.
Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women — 27-year-old Gabrielle Amarando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses — lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said in the press conference.
Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017. "Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said, adding "to date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered."
Amy McHale, who was previously married to Horsch's late father, has been missing since 2016. Blair Tonzelli, whose name appeared on the fake ID of the woman Horsch was stopped with in Center City, has been missing for several years.
Nicole Fusaro, who was 27-years-old when she was reported missing in 2018, was recently identified by police as the woman seen being strangled to death by Raymond Horsch in a disturbing video recovered during the investigation.
Two additional women—one around 25 years old and another not yet identified—appear in images as unconscious with signs of injury, according to investigators.
Federal prosecutors charged Eugene Horsch with being a felon in possession of firearms and unlawfully producing an identification document or authentication feature, according to court records. Raymond Horsch died last year.
A Philadelphia Inquirer report adds that the elder Horsch, a pornographer, had been known to use drugs and cash to lure women in addiction to his home to feature them in his graphic works.
Timeline:
June 2026: Horsch is arrested in Center City
Horsch was arrested after police said they recovered guns, drugs, fake law-enforcement equipment and identification documents during an investigation in Center City.
The arrest led investigators to an Olney property associated with Horsch.
Late June 2026: Police search the Olney home
Philadelphia police searched the home in the 400 block of West Chew Avenue, recovering weapons, chemicals, drug-related evidence, electronic devices and urns containing cremated remains.
Investigators also excavated parts of the property as the search continued.
August 2026: Police identify evidence linked to two missing women
Police said digital evidence recovered during the investigation appeared to show the bodies of Maribel Fresses and Gabrielle Amarando.
Fresses, 27, had been reported missing in 2018. Amarando, 22, disappeared in 2012.
Neither woman’s body has been recovered, and police have not publicly announced a cause or manner of death.
August 2026: Federal prosecutors take over Horsch’s case
Federal prosecutors charged Horsch with being a felon in possession of firearms and unlawfully producing an identification document or authentication feature.
Those charges are separate from the investigation into the Olney home. He has not been charged in either woman’s death.
By the numbers:
According to law enforcement, 58 people have been identified in digital images or videos recovered from the home.
Of those, five women seen on video or in photos appeared to be lifeless, while ten others are known to have died from overdoses elsewhere in Philadelphia.
Authorities said 16 people seen in various states in the evidence have been located and interviewed, although most have not shared details about what occurred in the house.
25 people identified as alive are scheduled for interviews, while three others have declined to speak with police.
Commissioner Bethel and FBI Special Agent Wayne Jacobs emphasized the massive scope of the review, describing a deliberate, methodical process to ensure evidence is handled properly and potential victims are identified.
Community impact and next investigative steps
What's next:
Special Agent Jacobs said investigators expect to return to the Chew Avenue residence in late September with a more focused approach based on new information.
Police plan to inform and engage with neighbors before future operations to minimize disruption.
"We will be on the block talking to the community to try to normalize this. As much as possible, it's going to be clearly disruptive, but we will be down on the community," said Bethel.
The investigation continues with help from the FBI and several branches of the police department, with further updates expected as lab results and digital analyses progress. A hearing on separate federal charges for Eugene Horsch is scheduled for January.
What we don't know:
Police have not found any human remains at the Chew Avenue property, and they have not been able to fully determine the fate of the missing women. The final scientific testing on the urns and chemicals remains incomplete. Investigators declined to share working theories about what happened to the missing women.
The Source: This article was written using information from the Philadelphia Police Department, FBI Philadelphia, federal court records, and prior FOX Local reporting. This story was reported from Orlando.

Title: JuJu Smith-Schuster's post-Chiefs career just got worse after Jets workout
Article_Text:
For too long, the Kansas City Chiefs have forced Patrick Mahomes to do all of the heavy lifting on offense. Either because their draft picks haven't always panned out or because their free-agent signings have been underwhelming, the team's wide receiver corps has often left plenty to be desired.
Andy Reid's offense is complex, so the Chiefs often resort to bringing disappointing veterans back just because of their familiarity with the system. But as much as Mecole Hardman or Marquez Valdes-Scantling might know the offense, they're not starting-caliber guys in this league anymore, nor were they for the majority of their time in Kansas City.
Watching JuJu Smith-Schuster fail to make the New York Giants' roster was already a telling sign of how bad things were in Kansas City in 2025. But now, knowing that he worked out for the Jets and didn't even get a deal, only made matters worse.
Chiefs 2025 playmakers have had a rough-go of it post-Kansas City
The Chiefs have done next to nothing to bolster the wide receiver corps. Rashee Rice is still a question mark, and Xavier Worthy might never live up to the hype as a former first-round pick. As for the rest of the supporting cast from a year ago, well, let's take a look.
Marquise "Hollywood" Brown was a healthy scratch in Week 1 with his new team. The Philadelphia Eagles could've used a veteran after trading A.J. Brown, but he's already behind newcomers Dontayvion Wicks and Makai Lemon in the pecking order.
As mentioned, Smith-Schuster is a free agent again. His best years are behind him, and with all due respect, you know a player has hit rock bottom whenever he works out for the Jets. Moreover, he left the building without a deal, meaning that the Chiefs' WR4 from last season wasn't good enough to play for a team that hasn't made the playoffs since 2010. Let that sink in.
Then, we have Tyquan Thornton, the only free-agent wide receiver the Chiefs retained this offseason. He drew a grand total of one target in the season opener and failed to record a single stat, so yeah, not ideal.
All in all, the Chiefs' wide receivers combined for five receptions for 37 yards in the Week 1 win over the Denver Broncos. The guys supposed to make Mahomes' life easier can't create separation, and those who played often last year can't even get on the field anymore.
Brett Veach has done a solid job of rebuilding the defense over the years, and it's hard to complain when the team has reached five Super Bowls (winning three) during his tenure. But that's also a testament to Steve Spagnuolo's defensive madness and Mahomes' greatness.
The Chiefs have one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time and just continue to trust him to make everyone look good. But if someone isn't good enough to play for the Jets, how is he supposed to take the field for this team?

Title: Dallas Cowboys vs Washington Commanders: 3 causes for concern in Week 2
Article_Text:
While it’s only Week 2, Sunday’s contest between the Washington Commanders and Dallas Cowboys is virtually a must-win for both sides. Since the 2015 season, just 14.7% of teams that started 0-2 (14 of 95) ended up making the playoffs.
Cowboys vs Commanders: 3 causes for concern in Week 2
The Cowboys desperately need a win this week.
After the poor display they put on the field in New York, the Cowboys have plenty to be concerned about in this matchup. With that thought in mind, here are three causes for concern in Week 2 against the Commanders.
1) Jayden Daniels’ rushing ability
The Commanders are expecting a big-time bounce-back from 25-year-old quarterback Jayden Daniels this season. After putting together one of the best rookie years in NFL history, Daniels had an up-and-down sophomore season plagued by injuries. If Washington wants any chance at making the postseason, they need Daniels on the field and at his best.
While Washington took a loss in their Week 1 matchup against Philadelphia, Daniels looked healthy and had a productive day against one of the NFL’s elite defenses. If the 25-year-old is healthy, he’s one of the most dangerous athletes at the quarterback position in all of football. Against Philadelphia, Daniels got back to using his legs as a weapon, rushing for 31 yards on five attempts.
This week, the Cowboys will need to place plenty of emphasis on taking away Daniels’ ability to take off and run. In three career games against Dallas, Daniels has averaged a little over 42 rushing yards per game. The whole world saw Jaxson Dart burn the Cowboys on the ground multiple times last Sunday, and you can imagine Washington is going to incorporate plenty of quarterback runs into their offensive game plan this week.
2) Washington’s ability to stop the run
One positive to come out of the Commanders’ Week 1 loss was how well they kept Philadelphia’s impressive run game in check. While the Eagles did record 136 total rushing yards on the day, 64 of those yards came on two runs by Saquon Barkley and Jalen Hurts.
If you take away Barkley’s big run of 42 yards, Washington held the talented running back to just 41 yards on 14 carries, an average of 2.9 Y/A. On the day, the Commanders’ defense ranked 10th in the league in defensive Rush EPA (-01.67) and third in defensive Rush SR (26.3%).
To avoid letting Dallas open things up in the play-action game, Washington will likely follow their Week 1 game plan against Philly and put heavy emphasis on slowing Dallas down on the ground. The Cowboys will need to execute better in the run game than they did in Week 1, when, as a team, they averaged just 3.8 Y/A.
3) 0-2 Potential playoff implications
As we mentioned at the top, falling to 0-2 is basically the kiss of death to your playoff hopes. To make matters worse, whatever team loses this game will not just have a 0-2 record overall but in the division as well. This would make it very difficult for that team to win any potential divisional tiebreaks come season’s end. Since 2015, only one team (the 2025 Chicago Bears) has lost their first two games of the season to divisional opponents and still went on to win their division that year.
It’s safe to say there will be plenty of urgency on both sides to win this game. With Dallas’ brutal upcoming five-game stretch, it is absolutely paramount they find a way to win on Sunday and avoid digging themselves into an early-season hole too deep to climb out of.

Cowboys vs Commanders predictions: Dak Prescott goes off

Title: MOD Pizza launches Abbott Elementary-inspired pizza
Article_Text:
Content Spotlight
The Technomic Top 500: Another tough year for chain restaurants
Top 500 chain restaurant sales slowed again in 2025 as consumers cut back on dining, but sectors like coffee, beverages and snacks and chicken thrived
The fast-casual chain's limited-time offer taps the flavors of Philadelphia, where the ABC series is based. Abbott Elementary's latest season is scheduled to debut on Oct. 7.
MOD Pizza has launched a new limited-time offer tied to the Emmy-nominated comedy Abbott Elementary.
The Seattle-based fast-casual pizza concept is offering a pizza inspired by Philadelphia, the setting for the ABC school-themed series. The show’s latest season is scheduled for Oct. 7, and will stream the next day on Hulu.
Dubbed The Honor Roll, the new pizza LTO has an olive oil and minced garlic base, topped with mozzarella, shaved beef with onions and green peppers, roasted red bell peppers and a finishing layer of cheddar cheese. The LTO will be available nationwide from Sept. 28 through Nov. 29.
“Abbott Elementary brings people together through humor, heart and a strong sense of community, which makes this collaboration such a natural fit for MOD,” said Charae Carter Jenkins, MOD’s vice president of marketing. “The Honor Roll is a fun way for our guests to join in the excitement surrounding the new season, whether they’re grabbing a pizza before tuning in or sharing a meal with fellow fans. We’re thrilled to bring a little bit of Abbott into MOD restaurants across the country.”
MOD has more than 440 units across 28 states in the U.S. and Canada, though the chain has been shrinking in recent years. It was acquired by Elite Restaurant Group in 2024 after closing 44 units. The closures continued into 2025, in what MOD officials at the time called a right-sizing of the portfolio for long-term growth.
The chain ended 2025 with 449 units, a nearly 7% decline, and $516.7 million in sales, down more than 10%, according to Technomic data.

Title: Buffalo Police crack down on speeders on 33 and 198
Article_Text:
BUFFALO, N.Y. (WKBW) — Buffalo Police are cracking down on speeders on the 33 and the 198, deploying a dedicated truck squad to pull over drivers going over the speed limit.
I went on a ride-along with Officer Mark Slawek as he patrolled the 33, clocking drivers and pulling them over for speeding.
After issuing tickets, Slawek explained the process to the driver.
"So, you've got to plead guilty or not guilty. If you choose to plead not guilty to this ticket, they reduce it to the equivalent of a parking ticket," Slawek said.
Then he went right back on the 33 to find the next driver.
Deputy Mayor Eugenio Russi, who oversees police and fire, said the Buffalo Police Department is making traffic safety a priority after hearing concerns from residents.
"Every time I go to a community meeting, one of the first things that comes out is, 'What are you gonna do about the 33? It's like a free-for-all there," Russi said. "We put together our unit, and we decided that we were going to tackle some of the stuff because this is what the community was asking for," Russi said.
Since the beginning of the year, Buffalo Police have issued more than 1,800 traffic tickets, nearly 800 of them for speeding.
Russi said the consequences for speeding are clear.
"You took it upon yourself to go over the speed limit. Then you're going to suffer the consequences for it," Russi said. "So slow down, follow the rules, please."
The truck squad's responsibilities go beyond writing tickets. Officers also escort oversized trucks through the city, including one hauling a massive generator from the Peace Bridge to Pennsylvania.
During his more than 3 decades on the job, Slawek has seen the deadly consequences of dangerous driving firsthand.
"The drunk driver came up over the Skyway the wrong way and hit them head-on at over 100 miles an hour," Slawek said. "The driver was killed on impact of both vehicles, and then the passenger had the engine compartment on top of her legs. She could not move, and the car started on fire."
"It's all over all day every day," Slawek said. "Speed kills."
The message from Buffalo Police is clear: slow down.

Title: NFL Week 2 Capsules

Field Level Media
                
19 Sep 2026, 04:25 GMT+10

Carolina Panthers (0-1) at Atlanta Falcons (0-1)
Sunday, 1:00 PM ET
FanDuel odds: Panthers -2.5, total 43.5
Series History: The Falcons lead the all-time series (37-25), but the Panthers have won four of the past five.
Carolina's offense exploded for 478 yards in Week 1 behind Bryce Young's 361 yards and three touchdowns passing, but turnovers and defensive breakdowns doomed the Panthers in a 59-37 loss to the Bears. Young has historically played well against Atlanta. WRs Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker and RB Chuba Hubbard give them multiple explosive options. Falcons RB Bijan Robinson has to be salivating after the Panthers allowed 291 rushing yards to the Bears. However, Atlanta didn't make a call at quarterback. It's likely Cooper Rush will make another start with Michael Penix Jr. (knee) possibly planning to return Thursday at Lambeau Field in Green Bay. Robinson, who posted 173 scrimmage yards in Week 1, has four consecutive games against Carolina with 100-plus yards from scrimmage. Atlanta struggled offensively in its loss to Pittsburgh, managing just 13 points and 238 total yards. Rush was particularly ineffective on third down, converting only 16.7% to first downs. Za'Darius Smith's two sacks and a strong secondary featuring A.J. Terrell and rookie Xavier Watts helped the Falcons stick around.
New Orleans Saints (0-1) at Baltimore Ravens (1-0)
FanDuel odds: Ravens -8.5, total 46.5
Series History: The Ravens have won four of the past five meetings.
The Saints went for two and the upset victory of Detroit in overtime in a one-point loss, but their offense came away looking like a winner. QB Tyler Shough's 410-yard, three-touchdown performance generated plenty of excitement around the young quarterback. WR Chris Olave had 182 receiving yards and New Orleans held up reasonably well in pass protection but did allow five sacks. Still, Shough was able to take consistent shots downfield. The Ravens overwhelmed Indianapolis in Week 1, generating turnovers and consistent pressure on Daniel Jones. Baltimore also put on an offensive show at Indy. QB Lamar Jackson appeared to have quickly mastered new play-caller Declan Doyle's scheme. Jackson threw for 324 yards and added a rushing touchdown, while Derrick Henry delivered a vintage performance with 144 rushing yards and three scores. Where Jackson will go with the ball on pass plays will depend on whether WR Zay Flowers (hamstring) is back in the lineup. Flowers posted a career-high 150 yards in Week 1 without playing a snap in the second half.
Minnesota Vikings (1-0) at Chicago Bears (1-0)
FanDuel odds: Bears -4.5, total 47.5
Series History: In the 2020s, the Vikings are 9-3 in this matchup. They swept the season series in 2021, 2022 and 2024.
Rain and wind could become a factor Sunday as the Vikings venture outside the dome for a second consecutive division matchup. Minnesota opened the season with a 39-22 win over Green Bay despite losing Kyler Murray (concussion) in the first half. Carson Wentz led the rally with four consecutive TD drives in the second half. Wentz had three touchdown passes and leaned heavily on WR Justin Jefferson, who finished with 92 yards and two scores. The Vikings did allow nearly 400 passing yards as they lived and died with the blitz, firing five-plus defenders into the pocket on more than 65 percent of their snaps. There will be a risk-reward balance at Chicago. The Bears put up 59 points with a dominant ground game producing six touchdowns. QB Caleb Williams said he's looking forward to the cat-and-mouse game with Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Williams had 269 yards and two touchdowns through the air and added two rushing TDs. D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai combined for 224 rushing yards. The Bears did not throw a perfect game defensively at Carolina and getting pressure on Wentz will be of significant importance.
Cincinnati Bengals (1-0) at Houston Texans (0-1)
FanDuel odds: Texans -2.5, total 45.5
Series History: The Texans have won four of the past five meetings.
Joe Burrow completed 71% of his passes and the Bengals generated 351 total yards against the Buccaneers, but they had their defense -- and three forced fumbles -- to thank for coming out on top. The Bengals had four sacks and four takeaways. They shift their focus to C.J. Stroud, who won't have No. 1 WR Nico Collins (hamstring) available. Stroud threw for 274 yards and two touchdowns in Week 1 while RB David Montgomery carried the offense with three TDs. The Texans can get to Burrow, but the issue last week was communication in the back seven. Houston was hammered by Josh Allen and the Bills for 409 total yards. With Collins out, the Bengals can tip the scales in their favor by handling Montgomery.
Pittsburgh Steelers (1-0) at New England Patriots (0-1)
FanDuel odds: Patriots -4.5, total 41.5
Series History: The Steelers lead 16-15; the Patriots have won three of the last four.
The Steelers let their defense do the dirty work in Week 1. LBs T.J. Watt and Alex Highsmith combined for four sacks, Watt had a pick-6 and the Falcons leaned almost entirely on RB Bijan Robinson for offense. The Patriots welcome back RB TreVeyon Henderson after he sat out Week 1 with an ankle injury. He brings a valuable speed and big-play threat, and QB Drake Maye could use a crutch after his three-INT opener at Seattle. Maye also lost No. 1 WR A.J. Brown (ankle) in the loss and Romeo Doubs didn't make a great first impression with costly drops. Steelers QB Aaron Rodgers (221 yards, one passing TD), back in Mike McCarthy's scheme, worked from the middle of the field to the sideline last week.
Green Bay Packers (0-1) at New York Jets (1-0)
FanDuel odds: Packers -3.5, total 44.5
Series History: The Packers have won three of the past four meetings.
There could be changes afoot on the Packers' offensive line. QB Jordan Love threw for 387 yards in a loss to the Vikings but felt pressure consistently. It might be too soon for major changes on defense, but coordinator Jonathon Gannon admitted this week Green Bay won't win games surrendering 39 points. WR Christian Watson looked the part as Love's go-to guy. He worked in the slot often, where his size and speed make him a nightmare for most defenses. Watson finished with 147 yards and two touchdowns. Second-year pro Matthew Golden added 95 receiving yards. The Packers are still searching for a rotation they can trust at running back with Josh Jacobs on the exempt list. The Jets opened their season with a convincing 23-10 win over Tennessee, highlighted by a balanced offensive attack and strong defensive play. Geno Smith was aggressive and efficient, completing nearly 80% of his passes. RB Breece Hall likely has Gannon concerned after he dominated with 118 total yards.
